scope: Five canonical Arrays and Regularity halls; final-text companion illustrations.

plates.title: THE SAME CUBE, COUNTED
plates.focus: An index persists after collection. Occupancy records, supporting floor cells and transformed display frames do different work.
plates.summary: One cube joins a row and a grid. Collection leaves its address; a wandering sphere changes the floor beneath the body. Nested frames can depart from sites that remain fixed.
plates.footer: Carry forward two separate questions: where is the slot, and what can happen at it?
panels: The row has a gap, and the count has not closed around it.

Two small matched before/after views of ONE ROW. BEFORE exactly four equally spaced cubes labelled [0], [1], [2], [3]. AFTER cube [2] and its suspended label have disappeared after visitor walks into it; retain exactly three cubes at the same sites, [0], [1], [3]. Do not renumber [3] to [2] and do not move cubes to close the gap. A small table shows [1,1,0,1].
Its entry in the table is now zero; the floor still names the empty place.

Close view within a four-by-four XZ pickup grid. Visitor stands by an EMPTY square plate marked [1,2]. Neighboring cubes remain; this label belongs to the plate and stays after collection, unlike row's suspended label. Small table reads grid_data[1][2] = 0. No cube held in the hand and no destination assigned.
What looked like an address on a diagram has become a place where your body can drop.

A light-blue sphere moves LOW over actual floor tiles, with one raised/copied dark block and a nearby consumed cell exposing a second support surface ONE METRE below. The visitor cautiously stands at the edge, not at a bottomless void. Use supporting image for copied-floor geometry. The agent's changes belong to the room grid, not the pickup table.
Pause after a change and walk around it.

Paired views of SAME floor from same angle: PAUSE retains raised blocks and one-metre hollows; RESTORE FLOOR returns that same area to level starting tiles. Fixed perimeter and thresholds remain intact in both. Sphere paused beside it; restoration is not caused by collecting row cubes.
Its surrounding frames can drift away, but the point stays at the indexed site.

Close view of ONE site in transparent nested-cube study: four nested wire cube frames displaced/turned/scaled relative to each other around an indexed fixed small GREY dot. A little ordered comparison has concentric aligned frames around SAME dot. Visitor shifts sideways; intersections separate in depth. This is Ada's spatial interpretation after Molnar, not a painting reconstruction. Avoid circles or solid sculptural spheres.
Their transparency lets us see through the structure without promising that we can read it.

Step back and see the nested-cube field layered into depth, controls showing DEPTH 1/4 then 4/4 as a small inset. Near and far edges overlap; foreground selected grey dot still anchored. Dense transparent frames in four layers, not an opaque cube block. Visitor looks for a site among lines; companion watches rather than lectures. Do not assert each crossing is a shared vertex.

plates.title: FLY INTO THE THIRD INDEX
plates.focus: Three indices address samples; a supplied enclosure grants flight. The cube record does not track the visitor, and formal regularity does not supply a history for hanging fragments.
plates.summary: A selected address lies above the ground. Flight lets a visitor reach it, but the zero left by collection records no body. Open forms and rough suspended fragments keep exact sites.
plates.footer: The third index has extended what we can address. Flight has extended what we can reach.
panels: You have named a place you cannot yet walk to.

Visitor at console OUTSIDE transparent glass enclosure. Readout [1,2,0] value 1. Selected marker contains a dark cube ABOVE ground layer, among a spacious four-across/four-up/four-deep cube lattice. Main foreground selected site clearly elevated; companion on ground. Keep ground entrance visible. Use image2 for marker/collection relations.
An indexed volume need not be a solid block.

Visitor flies/hovering inside enclosure, left controller aimed upward, no wings/jetpack, feet free of floor. Widely spaced cubes around, enough bodily clearance between samples. Flight belongs only inside glass frame; companion stays at ground doorway.
The gap is not an extra entry.

Visitor hovers between two labelled sites, neither site replaced or displaced. A thin overlay bracket says 2.4 m between sample CENTRES. Open space between occupied samples has no invented index plaque. Adult size unchanged; field not solid.
Your body could occupy the place without becoming part of this record.

Visitor hovers within selected transparent box where cube [1,2,0] has now disappeared INCLUDING its hanging label. Other cubes remain. Box selection stays. In a distinctly separated inset visitor has RETURNED to outside console, readout [1,2,0] value 0. Hovering body must NOT change readout back to 1. No cube gripped in hand.
The places remain; the diagonal succession settles into repeated columns.

Open skeletal cubic forms on a 5-by-5 arrangement. Small before/after diagram: changing RULE changes which of five open forms appears at each site, from diagonal succession to repeated columns. All positions remain the same; no solid filled cubes suddenly introduced. Show visitor following one row, not arbitrary infinite lattice. These are proposed rules, not a claim of exact LeWitt reconstruction.
What would the grid have to carry before its promise to hold something became a responsibility?

Rough fragments hang from slender supports at three distinct heights in a regular arrangement; use a cropped view rather than trying to enumerate all 75. Same sites appear before/after a roughness change on a small card. No simulated sag, collapse or damage history is added. The bodies look damaged, but this invented staging does not depict real demolition. Quiet visitor below lifted fragile-looking forms.

plates.title: A RULE UNDERFOOT
plates.focus: A small address-dependent instruction creates larger figures. Source motif, global rule and one local exception differ; black triangles are colour, not holes.
plates.summary: A four-by-four comparison makes one changed instruction visible. The same rule reaches a larger floor; an isolated extra turn changes one address while the support remains flat.
plates.footer: The unit that you notice need not be the unit stored by the program.
panels: A figure crosses the joints. No larger tile has been added.

Close floor-study desk: EXACTLY TWO square 4-by-4 samples, both using same unit square bisected diagonally black/white. BEFORE all sixteen triangles have the SAME orientation. AFTER address-dependent quarter-turns produce a joined figure across neighboring tile seams. Use Image2's two samples as geometry reference, not its dark rendering. Visitor presses APPLY/UNDO. No whole black/white checker cells substituted for bisected motifs.
The instruction has not grown longer. It is being asked again at more places.

Visitor and companion beside larger 16-by-16 flat motif field; restrained orange outline encloses exactly a 4-by-4 corner sample within 256 addresses. A short diagram card repeats rule (cx+cy)%4. Pattern, not floor height, changes. Main image high oblique lets small patch and larger field be read as SAME unit at more sites.
A local edit and a rule repeated everywhere need not have the same reach.

Visitor uses NEXT TILE. One outlined tile [1,0] receives 1 quarter-turn; nearby [2,0] receives 2 quarter-turns in explanatory inset. Other tiles remain identifiable. No enlarged unique master shape. Modulo chooses a turn count; zero is an orientation, not an empty cell.
One changed source can have different consequences under different rules.

Two comparison fields on flat floor, labelled TRANSLATE and REFLECT. A paired inset shows TURN MOTIF rotates the SAME diagonal source tile 90 degrees while their different placement/reflection rules remain. Visitor looks between fields. Reflection switches handedness in alternate columns, translation keeps orientation repeated. Never depict a moved wall or lifted tile here.
The same square is still here, turned once more than its neighbours.

One repeated translation patch with ONE EXCEPTION switched on: one clearly outlined bisected cell rotated by an extra quarter-turn; all neighboring tile orientations are identical and unchanged. Show an off/on comparison of the same patch; ONLY the selected cell differs. No new tile shape, hole or raised relief.
Your eye can find a ridge where your foot finds no step.

Low view of adult foot crossing a black-and-white pattern joint on COMPLETELY LEVEL floor. Strong optical chevrons appear sculptural, but foot rests on one continuous plane, with no raised triangles and no black voids. Companion sees visitor walk across freely. The printed colours cannot change collision.

plates.title: THE SAME RULE STANDS UP
plates.focus: The image's rules persist on another receiver; distance changes legibility. Turning one tile changes reading, while turning its supporting wall changes passage.
plates.summary: Patterns stand before the visitor. A chart makes distance and legibility felt; a hinged sheet reveals its plain back and a small constructed outside.
plates.footer: The first changed what we could read; the second changed where we could go.
panels: A field that was beneath your feet now faces you, rising well above your head.

Visitor in central aisle between tall five-metre black/white pattern panels with solid backing. Their repeating diagonally bisected square motif is same as previous floor. Image remains flat; no triangle-shaped apertures. Full-body scale and large pale hall.
The instruction remains exact at a distance where its work becomes difficult to read.

Pattern eye chart from Image2, exactly FIVE ROWS containing 1,3,5,7,9 copies respectively, decreasing sample size down chart. Every mark is the SAME 4-by-4 sample, not alphabet letters. Total25 marks. Visitor steps backwards, faint nearer pose overlay at side; rule console beside chart. Do not change the pattern while depicting distance.
Perspective is doing some of the work that we might otherwise attribute to the pattern.

Paired views of SAME fixed wall: face-on and oblique as visitor walks alongside. Pattern is not recalculated; diagonals project into different apparent angles. Thin explanatory camera/view arrows, no shape deformation, no new pattern generated.
The image has changed; the wall still holds you on this side.

At far end narrow tall sheet with each bisected motif stretched vertically, more than twice as tall as wide. Visitor presses EXCEPTION, ONLY one tile orientation changes on sheet. Wall stays closed; visitor's hand meets flat backing. Small caption button EXCEPTION; no door opening yet.
The opening leads onto a small landing outside the hall.

Visitor presses TURN WALL. That SAME entire patterned sheet quarter-turns about vertical hinge, with visible thin edge and image attached; open passage to SMALL floor landing and safety railing. Surface plus collision moves together. Distinguish motion of whole wall from previous cell-level turn. No sheet revolving while visitor occupies swept area.
Even this little outside has a floor and a rail.

Visitor safely on the limited outside landing looks back toward the sheet's thin edge and plain reverse. Companion visible INSIDE hall. Small landing bounded by rail, no floor extending beyond it, no implied next immense room outside. Seeing plain back reveals how little surface enclosed the earlier walk. Whole wall stationary open while visitor stays outside.

plates.title: A GRID WITH A CLOCK
plates.focus: Fixed addresses receive changing values. A retained musical score and an independently animated floor share a bridge but neither records the visitor's footsteps.
plates.summary: A foot stays while black and white exchange places. Triangles gather into larger figures. The sequencer and floor have separate clocks, with a sounding step able to brighten a column.
plates.footer: Sharing a space with a rhythm is different from being measured by it.
panels: Nothing has passed beneath your feet.

Two matched moments of a black/white checker floor: visitor's SAME FOOT at same square, fixed joints and level support. ONE STEP exchanges black and white across whole field. Small diagram phase 0 / phase 1 and (x+z+phase)%2. No rolling conveyor, translated tiles or literal moving floor.
The same two arrangements can alternate slowly or quickly.

Visitor beside floor console controls PLAY/HOLD, ONE STEP and SPEED. Held field with small two-frame alternation arrows. Increasing rate changes timing, not grid spacing or size. Body continues walking independently; speed knob does not push body or change footsteps.
The square joints still mark the old addresses, though your eye can join the triangles into another figure.

SUPER TRIANGLE: same diagonally bisected source motif from earlier halls now turning and joining. Two moments show a chevron then diamond spanning cells, per Image2. Visitor's one foot stays at a fixed joint through both. The surfaces are FLAT images; apparent diamonds are figures across cells, not new raised polygons. HOLD freezes intermediate picture only.
The grid keeps your choices; the playhead keeps returning to read them.

A step-sequencer station with sixteen step COLUMNS, multiple sound-track rows. Exactly two switched-on events in ONE track, remaining cells unlit. A narrow highlighted column is playhead. Adult turns one event off and another on to move its position; instrument row unchanged. Distinguish selected persistent event dots from transient highlight. Start from a blank small inset; no piano keys instead of grid.
The two clocks are separate, but the sound can still leave a visible response.

Floor console on HOLD: settled checker with one brightened column. Sequencer still plays, its highlight advances. Small paired view has sequencer stopped while floor continues animation; label FLOOR PLAY / SCORE STOP. Avoid a single master switch stopping both. Two separate circular clock overlays may explain timing, no physical clock objects invented.
The sequencer tells the addresses apart; that flash alone cannot.

Clean small comparison showing sixteen sequencer steps and TWELVE floor columns. Activate only step0, then only step12 in second-track paired moments. Both brighten floor column0. Diagram labels 0%12=0 and 12%12=0, same floor-column highlight, different score indices. Visitor walks nearby; no footprint sensors or score events written by feet.
